blocks.text: Having thus examined the passages of Scripture, the third argument by which we have proved that the hasida is the stork rests on the authority of many interpreters. For although we have shown by a long enumeration that most have gone astray, there still remain many for whom the hasida is the stork. Among these are, 1., those of the Greeks whom Olympiodorus refutes with worthless reasons: The stork, he says, does not lay its eggs on the ground. But neither does the ἀσίδα [asida], as he would have it, deceived by the version of the Greeks, who seem to attribute to the asida what the Hebrew text attributes to the ostrich. Nor is what he adds of greater weight, that τοὺς ὀρνιθιακὰ γράψαντας [tous ornithiaka grapsantas] distinguished the asida from the stork. For the Greek and Roman writers who treated of birds have nothing about the name asida, because it is Hebrew, not Greek or Latin. The others before Olympiodorus I do not regard, most of whom were entirely ignorant both of Hebrew and of the nature of birds. 2. To the Greeks we add the Syrians, for whom the hasida is ܚܘܪܒܐ hurba. So they render it everywhere, except in the passage of Job. Moreover, for the most learned of the Maronites ܚܘܪܒܐ is the stork ^{(5)}. 3. To these are added the Arabic translators of the Prophets, who in Ierem. VIII, 7. and Zachar. V, 9. have for hasida القعقع [al-qaʿqaʿ] alkoko, that is, the stork, not the crane, as Gabriel would have it, much less the magpie. For although القعقع [al-qaʿqaʿ] alkoko sometimes means the magpie, it also means the stork, and the matter requires that it be taken so here. Alcamus: القعقع العقعق وطاير اخر ابلق بري [al-qaʿqaʿ al-ʿaqʿaq wa-ṭāyir ākhar ablaq barrī] [III, 95] طويل المنقار والرجلين [ṭawīl al-minqār wa-al-rijlayn] Alkoko, the magpie, and another bird, pied, of the wild, with a long beak and legs. Damir, in one copy: القعقع طاير ابلق من طير الما طويل المنقار قاله الجوهري وابن سيدة وزاد وفيه بياض وسواد [al-qaʿqaʿ ṭāyir ablaq min ṭayr al-mā ṭawīl al-minqār qālahu al-Jawharī wa-Ibn Sīda wa-zāda wa-fīhi bayāḍ wa-sawād] Alkoko, a pied bird of the water birds, with a long beak. So Giauhari and Ibno-Saida assert; the latter of whom adds that this bird is marked with black and white. And in the other copy more explicitly: القعقع كلغلغ طاير ابلق ضخم من طير الما [al-qaʿqaʿ ka-laghlagh ṭāyir ablaq ḍakhm min ṭayr al-mā] Alkoko, the same as legleg (that is, the stork), a pied, bulky bird of the aquatic kind. So this is certain: that like some of the Greeks and the Syrians, so also some of the Arabs took the hasida for the stork ^{(6)}. 4. Nor do the more recent Hebrews of the last six hundred years render it otherwise. [col. 334] See especially R. Selomo on the Law; the same, and Kimchi, on Jeremiah; and Pomarius in his Lexicon. Accordingly, in the book entitled Masal Kadmoni, Fable 62, the speakers are הצפרדע והחסידה, that is, the frog and the stork, as appears from the picture. 5. Finally, the same is followed by the modern translators, Pagninus, Munster, Arias, Castalio, Junius, Piscator, the English, Dutch, Italians, French, etc., and among the lexicographers, Santes, Schindler, Buxtorf, etc. 6. Nor are there lacking those for whom the דיה לבנה of the Talmudists is not the kite or a white vulture, but πελαργὸς [pelargos], the stork: because, as דיה is formed from blackness and לבנה from whiteness, so the word πελαργὸς [pelargos] signifies a bird marked with white and black, as ^{h)} we have said. See Fuller, Miscellanea, book 6, chapter 10.

Now, if you compare this version with the rest, you will find it by far the best. For in all the others the fault is manifest. Thus in the heron, the coot, the swan, the kite and the ostrich there is nothing for which they should be named from piety. And, if you except the kite, none of them is migratory. The same judgement applies to the hoopoe. Nor do the coot, the swan and the ostrich nest in trees. And, however well the rest might fit, when one comes to the passage of Job, where the plumage of the hasida is compared with the feathers of the ostrich, I see no bird other than the stork to which this could apply [III, 96] ^{(7)}. These things we offer by way of example. For anyone who undertakes a comparison of the passages on the hasida will supply the rest for himself.
